Dermatology · published research

Dermal abrasion

A small sham-controlled human abrasion model found greater wound contraction after active treatment. Animal studies found improved healing measures with some wavelengths but not others. These results do not establish faster healing of routine clinical wounds.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A small sham-controlled human abrasion model found greater wound contraction after active treatment. Animal studies found improved healing measures with some wavelengths but not others. These results do not establish faster healing of routine clinical wounds.

Summary of the Evidence

Two direct “Dermal abrasion” papers are animal experiments, one in mice and one in cownose rays. A separate “Abrasion” record is a randomized experiment in healthy volunteers with induced superficial forearm wounds. This narrow mapping is a human wound model, not treatment of patients with accidental, surgical, or biopsy wounds. No standalone cell study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

Hopkins et al. randomized 22 volunteers in a triple-blind sham-controlled laboratory study. Each received two standardized 1.27-cm² abrasions, with active laser on one and sham on the other. On days 6, 8, and 10, both the treated abrasion and its untreated partner were smaller than sham-group wounds. This pattern makes the local contribution of light unclear and does not represent usual patient wound care (Hopkins et al. 2004).

Animal evidence

In mice, 810-nm treatment produced the greatest wound-area reduction, collagen accumulation, and re-epithelialization. Red 635-nm light also improved healing measures, while 730- and 980-nm protocols did not stimulate healing (Gupta et al. 2014).

A ten-ray study found no appreciable healing-time difference when PBM was used in multimodal care (Gilewski et al. 2024). Its model differs from the mouse wavelength comparison.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The mouse study tested 635-nm red and 730-, 810-, and 980-nm near-infrared light at 4 J/cm² and 10 mW/cm² for seven sessions. The human model used a 46-diode cluster spanning 660-nm red and 820–950-nm near-infrared light, 8 J/cm² at 700 Hz for about two minutes, repeated from days 2 to 10. These different models do not identify a transferable optimum.

Interpretation

The controlled human abrasion model found greater wound contraction with active treatment. In animals, 810-nm near-infrared light produced the largest reductions in wound area and greater collagen accumulation and re-epithelialization; 635-nm red light also improved selected measures, whereas 730- and 980-nm protocols did not stimulate healing. The human experiment used standardized superficial wounds in healthy volunteers, so effects in clinical wounds remain untested.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for contraction of experimentally induced superficial abrasions
Publications and records2 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A small triple-blind human experiment found greater contraction of standardized superficial abrasions after active treatment, while two animal studies differed by species and wavelength. The human result comes from a controlled model in healthy volunteers, not naturally occurring patient wounds. Independent replication in defined clinical wound types, with prespecified healing outcomes and reported dose, would support broader conclusions.
